Well, it's... it's a bit complicated to explain, but I suppose the main reason I’m here is because of what’s been happening at work. I’m a secondary school teacher, you see, and I’ve been doing this for a long time, so I know exactly how the administration communicates. I know the routine. But lately... well, I just can’t shake this feeling that certain staff emails and the morning announcements are actually coded messages about me. 

I mean, I’ll be sitting at my desk, grading papers or setting up my lesson plan for first period, and an email will come through from the principal or the district office. And the specific words they use, the phrasing... it just feels so pointed, like there's a hidden layer underneath the text that is meant only for me to understand. And then the morning announcements come on the PA system right after the bell rings, and it's the exact same thing, just broadcasting these subtle hints and directives about me to the entire school. 

I’ve brought it up with a few of the other teachers, and they’re very kind about it. My friend Diane in the math department even sat down with me the other day and gently pulled up her own inbox to show me that the emails were sent to absolutely everyone on staff. And I saw the distribution list, I really did, I know it went to everyone. But even seeing that with my own eyes, I just... I can't let it go. I can't shake the feeling that the core of the message is still somehow specifically about me, no matter who else received it. It's just been so exhausting to analyze every single morning, and it takes up so much of my mental energy when I should be focusing on my students, which is why I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to someone about it.

Well, it’s... like I was just saying, it really feels like it’s a specific message *about* me, rather than them trying to control my actions, like a puppet or something. It’s not that they’re trying to force me to do a specific task, it’s more that they are commenting on me, right out in the open, but hidden in plain sight. 

For example, when Diane showed me that distribution list on her computer—and bless her heart, she was so patient, sitting there in the math office during our shared planning period, scrolling all the way down the 'To' line just to reassure me—I saw all the names. I saw the entire faculty and staff on that list. But the *content* of the message... the way the principal phrased the reminder about, say, "maintaining professional vigilance during hallway transitions." I’ve been teaching for over thirty years. I know what a standard, generic administrative reminder looks like. But the specific words they chose, the cadence of the sentences... and then hearing the student reader on the morning announcements repeat that exact same phrasing about "hallway transitions" just an hour later... it just settles right in my chest. 

I know, I just *know*, it’s a message directed squarely at me, about my presence or my performance. It’s wrapped up in all this everyday school business, but the core of it is about me. And no matter how many times Diane or anyone else gently points out that it went to the whole faculty, or shows me the screen, that feeling... that absolute certainty that I am the true subject of the email... it just doesn't change. It won't go away. It’s just so incredibly draining to have to read between the lines of every single staff bulletin, wondering what they are really trying to say about me on any given Tuesday, you know?

Well, that’s... that’s the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? I mean, I *try*. I really do try to consider it. When I'm at home, sitting at my kitchen table with a cup of chamomile tea, trying to unwind after a long day of grading essays on the Industrial Revolution, I can look at it logically. Just last Thursday, after the email about the updated parking permits came out, I was practically vibrating with anxiety in the faculty lounge. And Diane, bless her, she saw me spiraling. She brought her laptop right over to my table, sat down next to my half-eaten turkey sandwich, and opened the email. She clicked on the details, expanded the recipient list, and walked me through it, name by name. She showed me the timestamp, she showed me that it came from the automated district server... she laid out all the logical proof right there in front of me. 

And in that moment, when she is showing me the screen, the rational part of my brain—the part with the master's degree, the part that has managed a classroom of thirty teenagers for decades—that part says, "See? It's just a generic email. It's not about you." I can acknowledge the facts she's presenting. But... and this is why I'm here, this is why I made this appointment... even when my colleagues gently show me they were sent to everyone, even when I see the proof with my own two eyes, I just can’t shake the feeling. 

It’s like there’s a disconnect between what my eyes are seeing and what my gut is telling me. I can consider the possibility that it's not about me for a fleeting second, maybe, but then the feeling just comes rushing back, stronger than ever. The certainty that the underlying message, the *real* meaning behind the words, is meant specifically for me. It just overrides all the logic, all the proof, all of Diane's gentle reassurances. It's like I'm trapped in this cycle where I know it sounds crazy, but I can't stop feeling it anyway. And it's just so exhausting to live like that, constantly battling my own intuition against the facts on a computer screen.

I know what a standard, generic administrative reminder looks like. It’s wrapped up in all this everyday school business, but the core of it is about me. It won't go away. It’s just so incredibly draining to have to read between the lines of every single staff bulletin, wondering what they are really trying to say about me on any given Tuesday, you know?\n\nDoctor: Do you think these messages are part of a larger plan or scheme that involves you?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s the thing, isn't it? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, impossible for others to understand... yes and no. I mean, the words themselves are just plain English, right? Like, anyone can read the emails or hear the morning announcements. Just yesterday, for instance, little Timmy from my second-period homeroom—such a bright boy, really, though he does struggle a bit with keeping his history binder organized—he was the one reading the announcements over the PA system. And he read this bit about "ensuring all classroom materials are properly stowed before the final bell." 

Now, to the rest of the school, to the students and the other teachers, they just hear a standard, everyday administrative reminder. They understand the literal words perfectly fine. But the *message*... the real, underlying meaning... that's the part that feels completely invisible to everyone else. And, like I've been saying, that is exactly why I came in to see you in the first place, because I just cannot shake this feeling—this heavy, persistent feeling—that these certain staff emails and those morning announcements at school are really coded messages specifically about me. 

The code isn't some complex mathematical cipher, it's... it's in the timing, you know? It's in the specific choice of the word "stowed" instead of just saying "put away," because I had just left a stack of graded essays on my back counter the afternoon before. So, when my colleagues... when Diane gently shows me her screen and points out that the email was sent to everyone on the staff list, or that the announcement was just a district-wide script... they think that proves it's not a code. They don't understand how it works. They just see the surface level of it all. 

They can't see the underlying thread connecting it to me, so to them, yes, that deeper message is impossible to understand. But for me, I feel the weight of it. I have this absolute certainty that it's directed at me, and it just... it doesn't matter how many times they gently show me that it went to everyone. It's like I'm the only one tuned into the right frequency to actually hear what's really being said, and it is just so isolating to be the only person in the building who understands what's really going on in these messages.

Oh, heavens, yes. I haven't always been... like this, constantly second-guessing every single word that comes out of the PA system. I mean, for years and years—decades, really, since I first started teaching at the high school—an email was just an email. I remember it quite clearly, actually. It was right around late October, just before the end of the first marking period. I was up to my ears in mid-term grading for my AP European History class—which is always a tremendously stressful time anyway, you know how teenagers and their parents get when their transcripts are on the line—and that's when it all really started to take hold. I was sitting at my desk, and the announcements came on, and suddenly it just clicked that they weren't just reading the daily bulletin anymore. And right around that same time, that's when I started catching myself replying to that voice. 

It’s just... it's been a very long four months, let me tell you. But before that? Completely, perfectly normal. I would just listen to the morning announcements, take my homeroom attendance, and dive right into the French Revolution without a second thought. I just want to get back to that, you know? Because living like this, analyzing every staff directory email for the past four months, it has just drained me completely.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, it's... it's a bit embarrassing to admit, really, because I am a very grounded person, or at least I always thought I was. But sometimes, usually when things have finally quieted down... you know how incredibly loud a high school can be, the lockers slamming, the teenagers shouting down the corridors, the bells ringing. And the thing that really gets me, Doctor, the thing that is so incredibly frustrating, is that it is so perfectly clear. It sounds as real as you and I talking right now. It is so distinct that I don't even pause to question it. I just answer her. I'm so used to colleagues or students popping their heads into my room after hours that my immediate reflex is to just respond. I'll say out loud, "Yes, just finishing up!" or "Can I help you?" because I just naturally assume it's Diane or maybe one of the custodial staff coming to empty the bins. 

And then... I turn around. I turn around fully expecting to see someone standing right there in the doorway or standing in my kitchen, and... nothing. The room is completely empty. I just stand there holding my whiteboard eraser or my teapot, realizing that no one is actually there. It's just me in an empty room, answering a voice that doesn't belong to anybody. It really throws you off balance, you know? Because in that split second before I turn around, I am absolutely, one hundred percent certain that another human being has just walked into the room to speak to me, and then I have to somehow recalibrate and remind myself that I'm completely alone.

Oh, no, no, goodness no. Never anything like that. I mean, heaven knows I get enough criticism in my day-to-day life—just last week I had a mother email me three separate times to complain about a B-minus I gave her son on a DBQ essay, if you can believe it—but the voice? I'll say out loud, "Yes, just finishing up the grading!" or "Just putting the kettle on!" because I am so thoroughly, completely convinced that someone—a colleague, a neighbor, someone—is standing right there behind me. 

And then I turn around, and... well, like I said, the room is just empty. It's just me. But to answer your question, no, she doesn't tell me what to do or say anything negative. It's really just those brief little observations when the house is quiet... which, honestly, is almost more confusing in a way. I feel like if she were yelling at me or telling me to do something strange, maybe I'd immediately know it was just my imagination, but because it's so casual, so everyday, I just fall for it every single time. I just answer right back to an empty room before my brain even has a chance to catch up and realize no one is actually there.

I can't shake the feeling that the core of the message is still somehow specifically about me, no matter who else received it. It's just been so exhausting to analyze every single morning, and it takes up so much of my mental energy when I should be focusing on my students, which is why I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to someone about it.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that these coded messages are meant to convey a specific message about you, or are they more about controlling your actions or decisions?\n\nPatient: Well, it’s... like I was just saying, it really feels like it’s a specific message *about* me, rather than them trying to control my actions, like a puppet or something. It’s not that they’re trying to force me to do a specific task, it’s more that they are commenting on me, right out in the open, but hidden in plain sight. \n\nFor example, when Diane showed me that distribution list on her computer—and bless her heart, she was so patient, sitting there in the math office during our shared planning period, scrolling all the way down the 'To' line just to reassure me—I saw all the names. I saw the entire faculty and staff on that list. But the *content* of the message... the way the principal phrased the reminder about, say, \"maintaining professional vigilance during hallway transitions.\" I’ve been teaching for over thirty years. I know what a standard, generic administrative reminder looks like. But the specific words they chose, the cadence of the sentences... and then hearing the student reader on the morning announcements repeat that exact same phrasing about \"hallway transitions\" just an hour later... it just settles right in my chest. \n\nI know, I just *know*, it’s a message directed squarely at me, about my presence or my performance. It’s wrapped up in all this everyday school business, but the core of it is about me. And no matter how many times Diane or anyone else gently points out that it went to the whole faculty, or shows me the screen, that feeling... that absolute certainty that I am the true subject of the email... it just doesn't change. It won't go away. It’s just so incredibly draining to have to read between the lines of every single staff bulletin, wondering what they are really trying to say about me on any given Tuesday, you know?\n\nDoctor: Do you think these messages are part of a larger plan or scheme that involves you?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s the thing, isn't it? That’s what keeps me up at night, just turning it over and over in my head. I don't necessarily know if it's a grand scheme, like something out of a spy novel, but... well, like I was saying before, I just came in because I cannot shake this feeling that these certain staff emails and the morning announcements are really coded messages about me. \n\nAnd it's just so frustrating, because part of my brain knows how it sounds. I mean, I’m an educated woman, I have my master's degree in education, I've been in the classroom for decades. I know how the school system operates. So when Diane—who really is just the sweetest woman, she’s been at the school almost as long as I have, we used to do the spring bake sale together before they changed the wellness policy—when she gently shows me her computer screen and points to the fact that the email went out to the entire staff directory... I see it. I see the names. I see the generic subject lines. \n\nBut it doesn't matter. It just doesn't matter what the screen says, because the feeling is so strong, so overwhelming, that the message is actually meant for me. It’s like the words on the page are just a disguise for the real meaning, and I'm the only one who can see through it. So, a larger plan? I don't know who would be planning it, or why the district office would care enough about a 56-year-old history teacher to coordinate with the morning announcement crew, but the feeling that they *are* doing it, that they are talking about me through these codes... it just won't go away, no matter how gently my colleagues try to prove otherwise. It's just so exhausting to deal with every single day.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered the possibility that these messages might not be about you, even for a moment?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s... that’s the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? I mean, I *try*. I really do try to consider it. When I'm at home, sitting at my kitchen table with a cup of chamomile tea, trying to unwind after a long day of grading essays on the Industrial Revolution, I can look at it logically. I can tell myself, \"Helen, you are being ridiculous. The superintendent does not care about you enough to hide a message in an email about the new recycling bins in the cafeteria.\" \n\nAnd then, of course, there's Diane. Like I've said, she has been an absolute angel through all of this. I just knew, I *knew* the way they phrased \"unauthorized vehicles in designated zones\" was a direct reference to how I handled that parent-teacher conference the week before. It just felt so pointed. And Diane, bless her, she saw me spiraling. She brought her laptop right over to my table, sat down next to my half-eaten turkey sandwich, and opened the email. She clicked on the details, expanded the recipient list, and walked me through it, name by name. She showed me the timestamp, she showed me that it came from the automated district server... she laid out all the logical proof right there in front of me. \n\nAnd in that moment, when she is showing me the screen, the rational part of my brain—the part with the master's degree, the part that has managed a classroom of thirty teenagers for decades—that part says, \"See? It's just a generic email. It's not about you.\" I can acknowledge the facts she's presenting. But... and this is why I'm here, this is why I made this appointment... even when my colleagues gently show me they were sent to everyone, even when I see the proof with my own two eyes, I just can’t shake the feeling. \n\nIt’s like there’s a disconnect between what my eyes are seeing and what my gut is telling me. I can consider the possibility that it's not about me for a fleeting second, maybe, but then the feeling just comes rushing back, stronger than ever. The certainty that the underlying message, the *real* meaning behind the words, is meant specifically for me. It just overrides all the logic, all the proof, all of Diane's gentle reassurances. It's like I'm trapped in this cycle where I know it sounds crazy, but I can't stop feeling it anyway. And it's just so exhausting to live like that, constantly battling my own intuition against the facts on a computer screen.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the people sending these emails or making the announcements are trying to convey a message that is unusual or impossible for others to understand?\n\nPatient: Well, impossible for others to understand... yes and no. I mean, the words themselves are just plain English, right? Like, anyone can read the emails or hear the morning announcements. And he read this bit about \"ensuring all classroom materials are properly stowed before the final bell.\" \n\nNow, to the rest of the school, to the students and the other teachers, they just hear a standard, everyday administrative reminder. They understand the literal words perfectly fine. But the *message*... the real, underlying meaning... that's the part that feels completely invisible to everyone else. And, like I've been saying, that is exactly why I came in to see you in the first place, because I just cannot shake this feeling—this heavy, persistent feeling—that these certain staff emails and those morning announcements at school are really coded messages specifically about me. \n\nThe code isn't some complex mathematical cipher, it's... it's in the timing, you know? It's in the specific choice of the word \"stowed\" instead of just saying \"put away,\" because I had just left a stack of graded essays on my back counter the afternoon before. So, when my colleagues... when Diane gently shows me her screen and points out that the email was sent to everyone on the staff list, or that the announcement was just a district-wide script... they think that proves it's not a code. They don't understand how it works. They just see the surface level of it all. \n\nThey can't see the underlying thread connecting it to me, so to them, yes, that deeper message is impossible to understand. But for me, I feel the weight of it. I have this absolute certainty that it's directed at me, and it just... it doesn't matter how many times they gently show me that it went to everyone. It's like I'm the only one tuned into the right frequency to actually hear what's really being said, and it is just so isolating to be the only person in the building who understands what's really going on in these messages.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of time where you didn't feel like the emails and announcements contained coded messages about you?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, yes. I haven't always been... like this, constantly second-guessing every single word that comes out of the PA system. I mean, for years and years—decades, really, since I first started teaching at the high school—an email was just an email. In fact, if I really sit down and trace it back, trying to pinpoint exactly when things shifted... well, the coded-message worries, the intense feeling that they are speaking directly to me, and... well, I suppose I should probably mention the voice I sometimes answer, too... all of that has really only been happening for about four months. \n\nI remember it quite clearly, actually. It was right around late October, just before the end of the first marking period. I was up to my ears in mid-term grading for my AP European History class—which is always a tremendously stressful time anyway, you know how teenagers and their parents get when their transcripts are on the line—and that's when it all really started to take hold. I was sitting at my desk, and the announcements came on, and suddenly it just clicked that they weren't just reading the daily bulletin anymore. And right around that same time, that's when I started catching myself replying to that voice. \n\nIt’s just... it's been a very long four months, let me tell you. But before that? Completely, perfectly normal. I would just listen to the morning announcements, take my homeroom attendance, and dive right into the French Revolution without a second thought. I just want to get back to that, you know? Because living like this, analyzing every staff directory email for the past four months, it has just drained me completely.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about the voice you mentioned you sometimes answer?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's a bit embarrassing to admit, really, because I am a very grounded person, or at least I always thought I was. It's sensory overload. It's a woman’s voice. And she doesn't give long speeches or anything theatrical like that. Usually, she just says my name. Just, \"Helen.\" Or she might make a very short, simple comment about exactly what I’m doing right then. Like, if I'm wiping down the whiteboard at the end of the day, she might just say, \"Erasing the notes.\" Or if I'm pouring my tea at home, she'll say, \"Pouring the water.\" \n\nAnd the thing that really gets me, Doctor, the thing that is so incredibly frustrating, is that it is so perfectly clear. I'm so used to colleagues or students popping their heads into my room after hours that my immediate reflex is to just respond. I'll say out loud, \"Yes, just finishing up!\" or \"Can I help you?\" because I just naturally assume it's Diane or maybe one of the custodial staff coming to empty the bins. \n\nAnd then... I just stand there holding my whiteboard eraser or my teapot, realizing that no one is actually there. It's just me in an empty room, answering a voice that doesn't belong to anybody. It really throws you off balance, you know? Because in that split second before I turn around, I am absolutely, one hundred percent certain that another human being has just walked into the room to speak to me, and then I have to somehow recalibrate and remind myself that I'm completely alone.\n\nDoctor: Does the voice you hear ever tell you to do something or criticize you?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, goodness no. Never anything like that. No, she isn't critical at all. And she certainly doesn't tell me to do things. Express my thoughts? Oh, heavens no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, I've always prided myself on being exceedingly articulate. You have to be, in my line of work. Well, staying on topic? No, not at all. I suppose that really goes hand-in-hand with what I was just saying a moment ago about being articulate. To be clear to others, you have to be perfectly organized in your own mind first, don't you?

But... and this is why I'm here, this is why I made this appointment... even when my colleagues gently show me they were sent to everyone, even when I see the proof with my own two eyes, I just can’t shake the feeling. \n\nIt’s like there’s a disconnect between what my eyes are seeing and what my gut is telling me. I can consider the possibility that it's not about me for a fleeting second, maybe, but then the feeling just comes rushing back, stronger than ever. The certainty that the underlying message, the *real* meaning behind the words, is meant specifically for me. It just overrides all the logic, all the proof, all of Diane's gentle reassurances. It's like I'm trapped in this cycle where I know it sounds crazy, but I can't stop feeling it anyway. Understand what I'm trying to communicate? Oh, no, absolutely not. I think I might have touched on this just a moment ago, but it really does bear repeating—I am exceedingly clear in my communication. If someone doesn't grasp what I'm saying, it is certainly not because of how I've delivered the message.

It's the exact same way with my sister, Martha. So, no, to answer your question, the message is always perfectly constructed on my end. I don't leave any room for ambiguity. I say exactly what I mean, and I mean exactly what I say. It's just so exhausting to deal with every single day.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered the possibility that these messages might not be about you, even for a moment?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s... that’s the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? The certainty that the underlying message, the *real* meaning behind the words, is meant specifically for me. It just overrides all the logic, all the proof, all of Diane's gentle reassurances. It's like I'm trapped in this cycle where I know it sounds crazy, but I can't stop feeling it anyway. I'll say out loud, \"Yes, just finishing up!\" or \"Can I help you?\" because I just naturally assume it's Diane or maybe one of the custodial staff coming to empty the bins. \n\nAnd then... It really throws you off balance, you know? Disconnected? My thoughts disconnected from each other? No, no, I don't think so at all. I feel like we are circling the same drain here, Doctor, because this is really just another facet of what we've been discussing for the last ten minutes. 

My thoughts are linked together perfectly. It's like a chain. Every single link is forged to the one before it and the one after it. You can't teach history—or function as an adult in society, frankly—if your thoughts are just floating around like disconnected little islands. Let's go back to the classroom for a second. If I am teaching the causes of World War I, I can't just throw out "Archduke Franz Ferdinand" and then jump to "trench warfare" and then suddenly start talking about the League of Nations without connecting the dots. The students would be completely lost! I have to draw the line from the assassination, to the complex web of alliances, to the mobilization of troops, to the stalemate on the Western Front. Each thought, each concept, leads inevitably to the next. It is a progression. A logical, undeniable progression.

And that's exactly how my mind works in everyday conversation, too. When I'm talking to you right now, every sentence I speak is built upon the foundation of the previous sentence. I don't just jump from topic A to topic Q without going through B, C, and D first. I suppose, as I mentioned earlier, I might spend a little extra time on C if I feel it's particularly nuanced or requires more background information, but the connection is always there. It is always deliberate. 

Even when I'm dealing with... well, with the stress of the evenings, when I'm trying to make dinner and that voice is just going on and on, my own internal monologue remains completely cohesive. I can be chopping onions and thinking, "I need to turn the heat down on the stove, and then I need to grade those essays, and I really hope Greg actually read my email about the buses." Those thoughts are all connected by the reality of my evening routine. They aren't just random, disjointed flashes. 

So, no, I have never experienced my thoughts being disconnected from one another. They are always firmly tethered together, creating a complete and sensible narrative. I really do pride myself on that, you know. It's so important to have a clear, connected mind.

The superintendent does not care about you enough to hide a message in an email about the new recycling bins in the cafeteria.\" \n\nAnd then, of course, there's Diane. Just last Thursday, after the email about the updated parking permits came out, I was practically vibrating with anxiety in the faculty lounge. It just felt so pointed. And Diane, bless her, she saw me spiraling. She brought her laptop right over to my table, sat down next to my half-eaten turkey sandwich, and opened the email. She clicked on the details, expanded the recipient list, and walked me through it, name by name. She showed me the timestamp, she showed me that it came from the automated district server... she laid out all the logical proof right there in front of me. \n\nAnd in that moment, when she is showing me the screen, the rational part of my brain—the part with the master's degree, the part that has managed a classroom of thirty teenagers for decades—that part says, \"See? It's just a generic email. It's not about you.\" I can acknowledge the facts she's presenting. But... and this is why I'm here, this is why I made this appointment... even when my colleagues gently show me they were sent to everyone, even when I see the proof with my own two eyes, I just can’t shake the feeling. \n\nIt’s like there’s a disconnect between what my eyes are seeing and what my gut is telling me. I can consider the possibility that it's not about me for a fleeting second, maybe, but then the feeling just comes rushing back, stronger than ever. The certainty that the underlying message, the *real* meaning behind the words, is meant specifically for me. It just overrides all the logic, all the proof, all of Diane's gentle reassurances. It's like I'm trapped in this cycle where I know it sounds crazy, but I can't stop feeling it anyway. And it's just so exhausting to live like that, constantly battling my own intuition against the facts on a computer screen.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the people sending these emails or making the announcements are trying to convey a message that is unusual or impossible for others to understand?\n\nPatient: Well, impossible for others to understand... yes and no. I mean, the words themselves are just plain English, right? Like, anyone can read the emails or hear the morning announcements. Just yesterday, for instance, little Timmy from my second-period homeroom—such a bright boy, really, though he does struggle a bit with keeping his history binder organized—he was the one reading the announcements over the PA system. And he read this bit about \"ensuring all classroom materials are properly stowed before the final bell.\" \n\nNow, to the rest of the school, to the students and the other teachers, they just hear a standard, everyday administrative reminder. They just see the surface level of it all. \n\nThey can't see the underlying thread connecting it to me, so to them, yes, that deeper message is impossible to understand. It's like I'm the only one tuned into the right frequency to actually hear what's really being said, and it is just so isolating to be the only person in the building who understands what's really going on in these messages.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of time where you didn't feel like the emails and announcements contained coded messages about you?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, yes. Well... doubt is a strong word, Doctor. I wouldn't say I've ever truly doubted it, not in my core. But... well, I suppose there are moments where I try to view the situation through an entirely objective lens, much like I teach my students to do when analyzing primary source documents.

Or that the morning announcements are broadcast to every single homeroom in the building. They try to show me the mundane reality of it. 

And in those moments, when Sarah is standing right there next to my desk, pointing at her monitor, I look at the screen, and I see what she sees. I see the "Reply All" list. I see the generic formatting. I understand the logic she is presenting to me. But... it doesn't change the feeling. It doesn't change the fact that when I read the specific phrasing in an email about, say, the new protocols for hall passes, I can see the subtext. I can see the layers of meaning that are directed squarely at me, regarding my specific movements and my specific schedule. 

So, while I understand on a purely intellectual level that these communications are distributed widely, and while I appreciate my colleagues' gentle attempts to ground me in their version of reality, I simply cannot shake the feeling that the messages are, at their core, about me. It's a very isolating experience, Doctor, to see something so clearly and have everyone around you looking at the exact same thing and seeing something entirely different. It’s... it’s why I’m here, honestly, because navigating that disconnect every single day is just exhausting.

Well, Doctor, I feel like we are treading the exact same ground we were just walking on a moment ago. We're sort of splitting hairs over the definition of the word "reality," aren't we? 

As I was literally just explaining to you, I came in here to see you precisely because of this agonizing middle ground I find myself trapped in. I cannot shake the feeling—the absolute, undeniable, visceral sensation—that these specific staff emails and those morning announcements over the PA system are coded messages directed at me. I know I just told you this, but it really is the entire crux of why I am sitting in this chair in your office today. 

When you ask if it's possible my interpretation isn't based in reality, you have to understand how incredibly frustrating that question is for me to process. Because, like I just said, my colleagues do try to help. Sarah will come over to my desk, and she will very gently, very patiently show me her computer screen. She will physically point to the "To:" line and demonstrate that the email was sent to everyone on the faculty list. She shows me the mundane reality of the situation. And I am an educated woman. I hold a master's degree. I teach advanced reading comprehension. I can clearly see the distribution list she is pointing at. I see her reality.

But the reality I experience when I actually read the text of the email... the very specific, deliberate phrasing they use... it feels entirely designed for me. It is a palpable weight. So, is it possible I'm wrong? I suppose anything is possible in a purely philosophical sense—which is exactly what I tell my seniors when we discuss epistemology and the nature of truth—but... no, I can't just dismiss my experience as "not real." I can't just turn off the interpretation. 

Even with Sarah standing right there, gently walking me through the logic and showing me it went to the whole building, the feeling that the message is fundamentally about me is just as real as the chair I am sitting on right now. It doesn't just vanish into thin air because someone points out a technicality about an email server. It is a constant, exhausting reality for me, day in and day out, whether anyone else in the faculty lounge sees it or not. So, asking if it's not based in reality just feels like an oversimplification of a very complex, very lived experience that I am desperately trying to manage.

It's like a chain. Every single link is forged to the one before it and the one after it. They aren't just random, disjointed flashes. \n\nSo, no, I have never experienced my thoughts being disconnected from one another. They are always firmly tethered together, creating a complete and sensible narrative. I really do pride myself on that, you know. Well... I suppose it depends entirely on how you define the word \"interfering,\" Doctor. I want to be perfectly clear: I am still teaching. I am still at the front of my classroom, doing my job, because my students rely on me and, as I've said, I am very dedicated to my work. \n\nBut... well, I will admit that the sheer mental energy it takes to process everything—deciphering the coded messages, and of course dealing with that constant, exhausting voice in the kitchen every evening—has left me quite depleted. Lately, I’ve actually needed some of my coworkers to step in and cover parts of those project lessons for me. It’s not ideal, but Sarah from the World History department has been very gracious about it. And the departmental planning meetings... oh, they can be so tedious, and they require so much administrative focus. I’ve really had to rely on my colleagues to help me get through those meetings lately, just to keep the agenda moving while my attention is, well, understandably divided by everything else I'm trying to figure out.\n\nAnd outside of work, honestly, my social calendar has just completely fallen by the wayside. I’ve always been a very active person, very engaged in my community, but lately... I’ve just stopped being reliable. I haven't been to my book club in weeks. They were reading a fascinating new biography of Catherine the Great, which I normally would have absolutely loved to lead the discussion on, but I just couldn't bring myself to go. I couldn't leave the house. It's the exact same situation with my community theater group—I've missed several of the weekend performances I had tickets for. And the neighborhood events, too, the block association meetings and the social get-togethers... I just haven't been attending. I simply don't have the bandwidth for small talk with the neighbors when I have these very specific, very pressing messages to decode. \n\nSo, while I am certainly still functioning and doing my job, I suppose you could say my extracurricular life has taken a rather significant hit. It’s a matter of prioritizing my energy, you see.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding it difficult to manage your daily responsibilities because of the coded messages and the voice you're hearing?\n\nPatient: Doctor, I... well, didn't I just answer this? When I speak to someone, whether it's a student needing help after class, or a fellow teacher in the faculty lounge, or even just the cashier down at the grocery store, I stay completely on point.
